t: Critical Assessment of the Literature

The sections above summarise what previous studies have reported. This section asks a different question: where those studies agree, where they conflict, what their methods can and cannot support, and what remains unanswered for the South Coast.
Where the literature agrees

Three findings recur across settings and methods and can be treated as reasonably secure. First, mud crab chains in the Western Indian Ocean are structured as a sequence of distinct functions rather than a single trading group, with harvesting, aggregation, processing and export performed by different actors (Mirera, 2017a; Jacinto, 2004; FAO, 2025). Second, survival of a live, perishable product governs value, so handling, containment and holding time are production economics rather than incidental practice (FAO, 2025; Mirera et al., 2013). Third, small-scale harvesters in the region operate with limited finance, limited organisation and limited access to formal markets (Béné et al., 2007; Fondo & Ogutu, 2021). The present study tests all three against a single dataset rather than accepting them as background.
Where the literature conflicts: the role of the middleman
The clearest disagreement in this literature concerns whether middlemen improve or reduce the position of fishers, and it is not a disagreement that can be settled by preference.

One line of work treats the middleman as a net cost to the harvester. Jacinto (2004) argues that in small-scale fisheries the share of final value captured at each node follows control of information and market access rather than physical effort, which implies that an actor positioned between the harvester and the buyer captures value the harvester cannot reach. Béné et al. (2007) extend this to credit: an advance against future supply solves an immediate cash problem while narrowing where the seller may sell, and they treat such arrangements as a mechanism of persistent low returns.

A second line reaches almost the opposite conclusion. Crona et al. (2016), working in Kenya and Zanzibar, describe middlemen as a critical social-ecological link whose accumulated relational knowledge is not easily replaced, and find them widely blamed for outcomes largely determined further along the chain while themselves operating on modest turnovers and carrying the mortality risk. On that reading, removing the middleman would not transfer their margin to the fisher; it would remove a function that has to be performed by someone.

The two positions are not reconcilable at the level of assertion, because they make different empirical claims: one about who captures the value, the other about what the middleman’s position actually returns once risk is accounted for. Resolving them requires the price at each node and the share each node holds, measured in the same chain. Neither study reports that for a Kenyan mud crab chain, and neither does the wider Kenyan literature. That is the first gap this study addresses.
Where the literature conflicts: what grading does

A second, less openly stated disagreement concerns grading. FAO (2025) treats grading by size, weight, shell condition and claw size as a legitimate quality signal that supports price formation in a live-crab trade. Jacinto (2004) treats the same practice as a site of informational asymmetry, because a criterion the buyer applies and the seller cannot verify transfers value rather than signalling it. Both may be right simultaneously, but only if the grading rule is applied consistently and both parties can read it. Whether that condition holds has not been tested in a Kenyan mud crab market; doing so requires recording which criteria each actor category actually uses, which this study does.
Methodological limitations of previous studies
Four limitations recur in the work reviewed above and shape what can be claimed from it.

The first is a production focus. Much of the Kenyan mud crab literature is biological, ecological or aquacultural: stock status, nursery habitat, growth and culture performance (Mirera, 2017a, 2017b; Mirera & Mosknes, 2015; Moser et al., 2005; Webley, 2008). This work is careful within its own terms but is not designed to describe exchange, and it cannot be read as evidence about prices, margins or bargaining.

The second is a setting mismatch. Where organisation and training have been studied, the setting has often been organised community aquaculture groups rather than independent capture-fishery actors (Mirera, 2014a). Findings about what groups achieve in an organised setting should not be transferred to a capture fishery where, as this study finds, no group exists at all.

The third is aggregation. Regional and national assessments describe constraints in finance, organisation and market access for small-scale fisheries as a sector (Fondo & Ogutu, 2021; Béné et al., 2007). Because they report at sector level, they cannot say which actor category faces which constraint, and therefore cannot indicate where an intervention should be aimed.

The fourth is the absence of cost data, which is a limitation this study shares. Munga and Muthumbi (2018) show for the Tana Delta that gross price differentials between nodes narrow considerably once handling and transport are netted out. Any study reporting gross prices, including the present one, must therefore stop short of claims about profit, and Section 5.6 states explicitly which market-structure dimensions that rules out.
The South Coast and Kwale County: what is and is not known

The literature specific to this coast is thinner than the regional literature and is weighted towards production. Mirera et al. (2013) document fishing tactics and traditional knowledge among Kenyan mud crab fishers, including the practice of holding crabs at home for several days until enough have accumulated for sale, which makes survival part of the marketing problem rather than only a harvesting one. Ochiewo et al. (2010) and Mirera (2014a) record the gendered division of the coastal fishery, with harvesting and first-tier trade male-dominated and women more visible in processing and trade. Fondo et al. (2020) describe the status of the mangrove mud crab fishery nationally, and Fondo and Ogutu (2021) place it within the Blue Economy agenda. Fulanda et al. (2009) and Kimani et al. (2018) supply the fisher population figures on which this study’s sampling frame rests.

Kwale County itself appears in this literature mainly as a location rather than as a subject. The one study that treats its institutions directly is Njiru et al. (2021), who examine the socioeconomic factors influencing trader participation in Beach Management Units in Kwale, and whose finding that participation varies with the trader’s own circumstances supports communication designed for particular actor groups rather than for the fishery as a whole. Beyond that, what is known about Shimoni, Majoreni, Vanga and Msambweni as markets, as opposed to as landing sites, is largely undocumented.

Three things follow. Prices at each node in a Kwale mud crab chain have not been reported; the grading criteria used by each actor category have not been recorded; and no study has tested whether actor characteristics, functions or constraints differ between the BMUs of this coast or are uniform across them. The regional and national literature supplies expectations on all three, but expectations formed at sector level cannot be assumed to hold at the level of a landing beach.
The research gap

The gap this study addresses is therefore specific rather than general. Previous work establishes that mud crab chains are functionally differentiated, that survival governs value and that small-scale harvesters are institutionally weak. It does not establish how the value of a South Coast mud crab is divided between the people who catch, trade and sell it; whether the grading rule that determines that division is shared or asymmetric; or whether any of this varies between the Beach Management Units through which the fishery is co-managed. Those three questions map onto the three objectives of this study, and answering them requires an actor-level inventory tested against site, which is the design adopted in Chapter Three.
